title: KPop Demon Hunters Nears Billboard Record for Most Weeks at No. 1
summary:
The KPop Demon Hunters soundtrack is on the verge of making Billboard history. It has spent 61 weeks at No. 1 on the Top Soundtracks chart — just one week shy of the record for the most weeks at the top.

The chart was introduced on June 30, 2001, so it doesn't include blockbuster soundtracks from earlier eras like West Side Story, The Sound of Music, or Purple Rain. However, it does include one classic: The Vince Guaraldi Trio's 1965 TV soundtrack, A Charlie Brown Christmas, because of its chart success after 2001.

KPop Demon Hunters has been No. 1 for all but four of its 65 weeks on the chart. It briefly yielded the top spot for one week each to Wicked: For Good, A Charlie Brown Christmas, Charli xcx's Wuthering Heights, and the soundtrack to the TV miniseries Heated Rivalry.

With a new record likely, Billboard looked at the 12 soundtracks that have led the chart for 25 weeks or more. The list includes two TV soundtracks and 10 film soundtracks. Notably, the five soundtracks with the most weeks at No. 1 are all from animated films.

Among the top contenders: the High School Musical soundtrack, which reached No. 1 in 2006 and spent many weeks on top; the A Star Is Born soundtrack with Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper, which hit No. 1 in 2018 and featured the Oscar-winning song "Shallow"; and the Frozen soundtrack, which dominated the chart starting in 2013. The Charlie Brown Christmas album also appears on the list.

Will KPop Demon Hunters break the record next week? Fans will be watching closely.
why_it_matters: Charts are how the music industry decides what counts as a hit, so a record like this shows how streaming lets a single soundtrack stay popular for more than a year and become a shared piece of culture for millions of young listeners at once.

background_read: Billboard (an American music-industry magazine that has published weekly popularity charts since the 1940s) runs dozens of different rankings, and its Top Soundtracks chart only began on June 30, 2001. That is why older hits like West Side Story (the 1961 movie musical about rival New York gangs), The Sound of Music (the 1965 musical about the singing von Trapp family) and Prince's Purple Rain (a 1984 film and album) are not counted on it.
Soundtrack albums became big business from the 1970s onwards, when a hit film such as Saturday Night Fever could send its album to the top of the main Billboard 200 chart as well.

Animated films have an especially strong record on this chart: Disney's Frozen (2013) stayed near the top for months thanks to the song "Let It Go", and High School Musical (2006) became a teen phenomenon through a Disney Channel TV movie.
A soundtrack keeps charting for as long as people keep streaming or buying its songs, so family films that each new generation of children watches again and again tend to have unusual staying power.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — fans and the film's creators
perspectives.description: For the artists behind the soundtrack, 61 weeks at No. 1 proves the music has outlived the film's release and become part of daily life. Fans see it as a win for a style of pop that blends Korean and Western sounds, and for animated films that are usually treated as less serious than live-action hits.

Critics point out that the chart only starts in 2001, so calling anything the 'most weeks ever' ignores decades of legendary albums. Others argue that modern charts reward endless streaming playlists rather than the intense, short bursts of buying that older records were built on.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — analysts of the music business
perspectives.description: Analysts see this as a pattern: since charts switched from sales to streams, a handful of soundtracks dominate for far longer because new young viewers discover the same songs year after year. Animated family films fit that model better than almost anything else.

If the record falls, other animated soundtracks will try to follow the same path, and Billboard may face pressure to explain or even adjust how long-running records are counted. Fans will also expect the next big animated hit to chase the same milestone.
